Isle of Skye: The Ultimate Motorcycle Riding Guide

The Isle of Skye is Scotland's most visited island and one of the most spectacular motorcycle destinations in Britain. The Cuillin mountains, the Trotternish Ridge, sea lochs, and dramatic coastal cliffs create a landscape of extraordinary drama. The roads are narrow, the scenery is vast, and the experience is unforgettable.

Getting to Skye

  • Skye Bridge (free): The A87 from Kyle of Lochalsh crosses the bridge to Kyleakin. No toll since 2004.
  • CalMac ferry (Mallaig to Armadale): A scenic alternative approaching from the south. The crossing takes 30 minutes and the approach to Mallaig through the Silver Sands is beautiful.

The Trotternish Peninsula

The northern loop of Skye contains its most famous landmarks:

  • The Old Man of Storr: A 160ft rock pinnacle visible from the A855. The car park is a short drive from Portree. A 45-minute walk takes you to the base.
  • The Quiraing: Otherworldly landscape of rock pinnacles, cliffs, and plateaus. The single-track road across the Trotternish Ridge is one of Scotland's most dramatic — views in every direction are staggering.
  • Kilt Rock and Mealt Falls: A sea cliff resembling a pleated kilt, with a waterfall dropping directly into the sea. Viewpoint right beside the road.

The Cuillins

The Black Cuillin ridge is the most dramatic mountain range in Britain. The road from Sligachan to Elgol follows the coast of Loch Scavaig with the Cuillins rising behind — a stunning ride and an essential Skye experience.

Western Skye

  • Neist Point: Skye's most westerly point. A 30-minute walk from the car park to the lighthouse on dramatic cliffs. The sunset views are legendary.
  • Dunvegan Castle: The oldest continuously inhabited castle in Scotland. The loch setting is beautiful.
  • Talisker Distillery: On the shores of Loch Harport. Tours and tasting available — but not if you're riding afterwards.
Skye's roads are single-track in many places. In summer, traffic can be heavy with campervans and tour coaches. Use passing places correctly (pull left for oncoming, don't use them for overtaking), be patient, and enjoy the enforced slow pace. Skye isn't meant to be rushed.

Practical Tips

  • Fuel in Portree, Broadford, and Dunvegan. Fill up when you can — distances between stations are significant.
  • Book accommodation in advance during summer. Skye is extremely popular and options fill up fast.
  • Midges are fierce from June to September. Carry repellent and a head net.
  • Weather is highly changeable. Pack waterproofs and be prepared for rain, mist, and wind at any time.
  • Allow 2-3 days to see Skye properly. One day is a rush — you'll only skim the surface.
keyTakeaways: Skye is reached free via the Skye Bridge (A87) from Kyle of Lochalsh, or by the scenic CalMac ferry from Mallaig to Armadale.
The Trotternish Peninsula holds Skye's famous landmarks: the Old Man of Storr, the Quiraing and Kilt Rock.
The single-track road across the Trotternish Ridge to the Quiraing is one of Scotland's most dramatic.
Roads are single-track in many places; use passing places correctly, pull left for oncoming, never overtake in them.
Allow two to three days to see Skye properly, fuel at Portree, Broadford and Dunvegan, and carry midge protection June to September.

faq.q: How do I get to Skye on a motorcycle?
faq.a: You have two options. The Skye Bridge carries the A87 from Kyle of Lochalsh to Kyleakin and has been free of tolls since 2004. Alternatively, the CalMac ferry from Mallaig to Armadale is a scenic 30-minute crossing approaching from the south, with a beautiful run through the Silver Sands to reach Mallaig. Both make excellent ways onto the island.

faq.q: How should I handle Skye's single-track roads?
faq.a: Many of Skye's roads are single-track. Use passing places correctly: pull into the one on your left for oncoming traffic, and never use them for overtaking. In summer, traffic can be heavy with campervans and tour coaches, so be patient and enjoy the enforced slow pace. Skye is not meant to be rushed, and the scenery rewards a relaxed approach.

faq.q: How long do I need for Skye?
faq.a: Allow two to three days to see Skye properly. One day is a rush and you will only skim the surface. That time lets you ride the Trotternish loop for the Old Man of Storr and the Quiraing, reach Elgol beneath the Cuillins, and walk out to Neist Point for its legendary sunset. Book accommodation well in advance during summer, as Skye is extremely popular.

faq.q: What should I pack for weather and midges?
faq.a: Skye's weather is highly changeable, so pack waterproofs and be prepared for rain, mist and wind at any time. Midges are fierce from June to September, so carry repellent and a head net for stops. Fuel is available in Portree, Broadford and Dunvegan, and you should fill up when you can because distances between stations are significant across the island.
